extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and limits for using inductive methods, designing/verifying scientific hypotheses, and interpreting experiments and statistical evidence in scientific and social inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The law that causes composing together produce combined effects (duplication of causes tends to double effect), subject to considerations of immediate vs remote effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent exceptions often arise from attending to the remote instead of the immediate effect; duplicating a cause commonly duplicates the immediate collocation even when the observed ultimate effect is not doubled because of saturation or dependence on subsequent conditions. Consider immediate mechanical/physical changes (collocation) produced by causes when evaluating composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collocation/saturation exception to Composition of Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases where causes 'merely make good the collocation for bringing a prime mover into action' (e.g., pointing a gun, a single sufficient spark, a dose of medicine) seem to violate simple composition rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are not true exceptions: the immediate effect (the collocation) is duplicated by adding causes, but once a certain collocation suffices to produce the whole effect at that time/place, further duplication does not increase that effect. Doubling with difference of time/place (e.g., two guns fired separately) does double effect. Consider remote vs immediate effects and possible heteropathic (qualitatively different) remote effects when doses are increased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check whether the consequent was produced by the means of producing the antecedent
rubrics_metrics.description: A consequent might be generated not by the antecedent itself but by the means employed to produce that antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since means are usually under our power and (to an extent) within our knowledge, we should judge whether the means could have produced the consequent independently; this assessment reduces misattribution of causation to the antecedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of natural experiments employing complex means
rubrics_metrics.description: When Nature produces an experimental-like circumstance by complex means which we cannot fully analyze (e.g., clearing off a canopy of clouds), the natural experiment is of little value except to corroborate conclusions already obtained by other methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the process used by Nature is itself insufficiently understood, we cannot be sure whether the observed effect is due to the purported cause or to some unknown agency of the means; treat such natural experiments as subordinate corroboration, not primary proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of the Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: If a cause varies alone and the effect varies alone, one has strong evidence of connection; concomitant variations can single out causes even under complication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method is useful (e.g., appetite increases with cold, tides variation with sun/moon positions, elimination of nitrogen with muscular exercise). But when many influencing causes exist without a predominant one, or several are continually changing, it's scarcely possible to trace the relation between variations of effect and any single cause to assign its real share.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental methods less reliable in complex combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments and observation are the ultimate basis of knowledge, but experimental methods are often illusory when dealing with complex combinations (e.g., particular medical treatments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experiment to ascertain general laws (e.g., nerve functions discovered via animal experiments), but in complex systems rely on deductive investigation to disentangle interacting causes. Recognize experiments' limits in complex practical applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of Explanation equal limits of Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific explanation and inductive generalization are the same; the limits of explanation are the limits of induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction presupposes similarity among phenomena and reduces similar phenomena under a common statement. Generalization is legitimate only when phenomena are sufficiently similar and the putative cause can be shown to produce them according to the same law; otherwise the unity of cause is only a nominal guess and adds no real explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that a proposed unified cause produce phenomena under the same law
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when phenomena are not generically distinct and it is legitimate to seek a single cause, success requires showing the cause is capable of producing the phenomena according to the same law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two kinds of phenomena (e.g., gravity and cohesion) agree in only one respect but differ widely in how they vary with distance or material, uniting them under one cause is futile and may be merely nominal; the cause must explain the phenomena in the same terms/law to be a legitimate generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of hypotheses: deduce consequences and compare with facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses are legitimate scientific tools when their consequences can be deduced and tested against facts; they need not be proved immediately but must be testable and refutable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Broussais' localization hypothesis, Gilbert's earth-as-magnet, brain-as-voltaic-pile, Gall's phrenology, Darwin's natural selection. A hypothesis is justified if deducing consequences and comparing with observable facts allows disproof when ill-founded; hypotheses that are 'vera causa' and capable of producing effects of the same kind are especially valuable for guiding inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vera causa criterion for hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis especially merits consideration when it is a 'vera causa', i.e., a cause shown to be capable (in principle) of producing effects of the same kind as those ascribed to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The question of possibility for a hypothesis is often one of degree; fulfilling the conditions of hypothesis (deducing consequences and comparing with facts) is sufficient to render a bold suggestion admissible for scientific discussion even before proof by induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: First instance establishes possibility; repetition indicates control/invariability
rubrics_metrics.description: The first occurrence of an event is especially important because it proves possibility (shows there exists a cause adequate to it); subsequent instances indicate the intensity, extent, and invariability of that cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reason from one instance to the next without reference to the underlying cause; use the first instance to establish possibility and further instances to estimate how well-controlled or invariable the cause is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probabilistic inference depends on stability of causal collocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Probabilities and empirical calculations of chances are valid only under the continuance of the same collocation of causes; if the causes have changed, past frequency does not determine future probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insurance and many calculations rest on empirical frequency comparisons, but no theory of chances can infer future probabilities if the underlying causes have undergone changes. Empirical certainty is conditional on the continuance of the same causal conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate statistical estimation for inductive inquiry (mean vs average)
rubrics_metrics.description: For inductive purposes the 'mean' is not simply the arithmetical average; the most probable determination of invariable elements from observation is that which minimizes the sum of the squares of individual deviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deviations are asymmetric (many small deviations on one side and few large on the other), the arithmetic average may misrepresent the invariable cause's effect. Use principles such as least-squares (sum of squares minimal) for probable determination, following Herschel/Quetelet accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about simple recitals of instances in political/economic proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to prove economic or political doctrines by a recital of instances are often futile because circumstances in individual cases are rarely fully stated and counter-instances are omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single sudden agent-change followed by an effect (e.g., diplomatic rupture followed by money-market derangement) is inconclusive as an experiment; experiments in politics can only verify a deduction when backed by knowledge of motives and by historical ascertainment of many instances with due precautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy alone does not validate a hypothesis (case of luminiferous ether)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogies (e.g., light's travel, time-delay, interception being analogous to mechanical undulations) support a hypothesis but do not prove it; one must not assume the only possible mechanism is the analogous one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even striking analogies do not allow one to assume that the underlying mechanism is identical; hypotheses suggested by analogy must still be evaluated on whether they can truly exhibit the attribute(s) in question and be rendered amenable to observation/experiment.
